catalog_quote: An important word syllabification pattern for Bih is the “sesquisyllabic” structure (Matisoff, 1973) in which a canonical word consists of a reduced „pre-tonic‟ (presyllable) and a main „tonic‟ syllable. ... Thus, the main syllable has the larger inventory of phonemes. Plus, the main syllable displays the whole set of possible phonological contrasts. Austronesian languages are often disyllabic with penultimate stress (Thurgood, 1999, p. 60). Chamic languages with the influence of Mon-khmer stress pattern (which is iambic--weak and strong stress patterns) reduce or even drop the vowel in the presyllable results in iambic stress patterns. The iambic stress patterns then leads to the development of monosyllabic word structure with two-consonant initial clusters throughout Chamic languages (p.61). Even though Bih still retains disyllabic words from PC, it is adapted to the iambic stress pat…

audit.reasoning: The classification (final/main-syllable prominence in a sesquisyllabic iambic word, rule 01, right edge) rests on the only existing reference grammar of Bih (Nguyen 2013, 352 pp., fieldwork-based), which we hold as PDF and text; the deciding quotation is verbatim at sec. 3.2 pp. 21-22 with Figure 3.1, and the supporting presyllable-reduction facts are at sec. 3.3.1. No better or competing description of Bih prosody exists in Glottolog or on the open web, so there is nothing to add to the list of works to obtain and no reason to reclassify. The only caveat, already implicit in the record, is that the source states the iambic pattern typologically/structurally rather than with an explicit 'stress falls on the final syllable' sentence or acoustic evidence.
